snippet.title: Pompeii on Its Last Morning — An AI Reconstruction of August 24, 79 AD
snippet.description:
What did Pompeii actually look like on the morning it was destroyed?

Not the ruins. Not the museum displays. The living city — with its painted walls, crowded streets, public fountains, fast food counters, and twenty thousand people who had no idea what was about to happen.

In this video, I use modern AI tools to reconstruct Pompeii as it may have appeared in its final hours on August 24, 79 AD — from the bustling Forum and the Stabian Baths to the amphitheatre and the streets where ordinary life carried on until Vesuvius ended everything.

This is not a dramatization. It is an honest attempt to bring back, as closely as possible, a world that was buried under six meters of volcanic ash and forgotten for seventeen centuries.

snippet.title: 300 Bodies. Hidden for 2,000 Years. | The City More Preserved Than Pompeii
snippet.description:
HERCULANEUM. August 24th, 79 AD.

For 300 years, scientists believed everyone escaped.

They were wrong.

In 1980, archaeologists excavating the ancient shoreline found 300 people hidden in the boathouses. Waiting for rescue that never came. Their skulls had exploded. Their brains had turned to glass.

They died in less than one second.

Herculaneum is not Pompeii. It is smaller. Less famous. Visited by one tenth as many people.

And yet every archaeologist who has worked both sites will tell you the same thing.

Herculaneum is more extraordinary.

Wooden door frames still in place after 2,000 years. A carbonized loaf of bread still showing the marks where it was scored before baking. A fishing net. A wooden cradle. The meal that was never eaten.

And beneath it all — 1,800 papyrus scrolls sealed since 79 AD. Being read for the first time right now. In 2026.

This is what Herculaneum really looked like. Before Vesuvius ended everything.

Step into Pompeii on October 24, 79 AD—hours before Mount Vesuvius erupted and buried the city under 20 feet of ash.

Using AI reconstruction and archaeological evidence, we've brought ancient Pompeii back to life. Watch the Forum bustling with 15,000 Romans. See the amphitheater—the oldest stone amphitheater in the world. Walk through the Forum Baths with their advanced hypocaust heating system. Experience the streets, the markets, the temples—all frozen in time by the catastrophic eruption.

This isn't the ruins you see today. This is Pompeii as it actually was—a thriving Roman city at the peak of its power, minutes before disaster struck.

🏛️ IN THIS VIDEO:
- The Forum - Political and religious center of Pompeii
- Temple of Jupiter - Massive columns and sacred architecture

- Population: 11,000-15,000 people

- Rediscovered: 1748, after being lost for 1,700 years

This reconstruction is based on decades of archaeological excavations, ancient texts from Pliny the Younger (the only eyewitness account), and cutting-edge AI technology to visualize what the ruins looked like when they were whole.

snippet.title: La presa di Roma (1905) Filoteo Alberini
snippet.description:
_*La presa di Roma*_ è un film del 1905 di *Filoteo Alberini* . La pellicola risulta essere il  film italiano della storia del cinema. Diviso in 7 quadri, il film è  una ricostruzione storica dell'episodio risorgimentale della breccia di Porta Pia, che permise all'esercito piemontese di entrare in città e annettere Roma al Regno d'Italia:

_Capitoli_
00:00 - Titoli
00:13 - 1. Il parlamentario Generale Carchidio a Ponte Milvio 
01:07 - 2. Dal Generale Kanzler – Niente resa! 
02:47 - 3. Al campo dei bersaglieri – All’armi! 
03:02 - 4. L’ultima cannonata, perduto
03:16 - 5. La breccia a Porta Pia – All’assalto! 
04:02 - 6. Bandiera bianca, perduto
04:14 - 7. Apoteosi, perduto

Dei sette quadri girati ne sono sopravvissuti solamente tre, ovvero il primo, il secondo ed il quinto.
Il film fu proiettato per la prima volta in pubblico proprio nel giorno dell'anniversario della Presa di Roma: il 20 settembre 1905. 

#FiloteoAlberini #presadiroma #cinemaitaliano 

*Filoteo Alberini* (n. 1865, Orte – m. 1937, Roma, Italia) è un regista italiano. Tra i precursori del cinematografo in Italia, Alberini inventa una macchina per le riprese, il _Kinetografo Alberini_ , nello stesso anno dei Fratelli Lumière che, purtroppo per lui, depositeranno il brevetto prima che egli riesca nell’impresa; nel 1905 crea la compagnia che nel 1906 prenderà il nome di *Cines* e che nel 1913 produrrà il primo film colossal italiano della storia _*Quo vadis?*_ .

Musica di Aufklaurung

snippet.title: Walk around in a 3D splendid house from the ancient Pompeii
snippet.description:
By combining traditional archaeology with 3D technology, researchers at Lund University in Sweden have managed to reconstruct a house in Pompeii to its original state before the volcano eruption of Mount Vesuvius thousands of years ago. Unique video material has now been produced, showing their creation of a 3D model of an entire block of houses. 

After the catastrophic earthquake in Italy in 1980, the Pompeii city curator invited the international research community to help document the ruin city, before the state of the finds from the volcano eruption in AD 79 would deteriorate even further. The Swedish Pompeii Project was therefore started at the Swedish Institute in Rome in 2000. The researcher in charge of the rescue operation was Anne-Marie Leander Touati, at the time director of the institute in Rome, now Professor of Classical Archaeology and Ancient History at Lund University.

Since 2010, the research has been managed by the Department of Archaeology and Ancient History in Lund. The project now also includes a new branch of advanced digital archaeology, with 3D models demonstrating the completed photo documentation. The city district was scanned during the field work in 2011–2012 and the first 3D models of the ruin city have now been completed. The models show what life was like for the people of Pompeii before the volcano eruption of Mount Vesuvius. The researchers have even managed to complete a detailed reconstruction of a large house, belonging to the wealthy man Caecilius Iucundus.

“By combining new technology with more traditional methods, we can describe Pompeii in greater detail and more accurately than was previously possible”, says Nicoló Dell´Unto, digital archaeologist at Lund University.

Among other things, the researchers have uncovered floor surfaces from AD 79, performed detailed studies of the building development through history, cleaned and documented three large wealthy estates, a tavern, a laundry, a bakery and several gardens. In one garden, they discovered that some of the taps to a stunning fountain were on at the time of eruption – the water was still gushing when the rain of ash and pumice fell over Pompeii.

The researchers occasionally also found completely untouched layers. In a shop were three, amazingly enough, intact windows (made out of translucent crystalline gypsum) from Ancient Rome, stacked against each other. By studying the water and sewer systems they were able to interpret the social hierarchies at the time, and see how retailers and restaurants were dependent on large wealthy families for water, and how the conditions improved towards the end, before the eruption.

An aqueduct was built in Pompeii, enabling residents to no longer having to rely on a few deep wells or the tanks of collected rainwater in large wealthy households.

The work behind the 3D film and a discussion on the credibility of the reconstructions are presented in an article, published in SCIRES Italy. 

Istituto di Scienza e Tecnologie dell'Informazione and the Humanities Lab at Lund University have contributed to the development of the material and 3D work.

###
Article: Reconstructing the Original Splendour of the House of Caecilius Iucundus. A Complete Methodology for Virtual Archaeology Aimed at Digital Exhibition.

snippet.title: The Truth about the Pompeii Bodies
snippet.description:
Are the Pompeii Bodies Real? In this video you'll find out how the Pompeii Bodies were preserved and what was preserved. 

It all started when Giuseppe Fiorelli was appointed to oversee the excavations of Pompeii in 1863. 

He noticed something unusual: there were hollow voids in the hardened volcanic ash. He soon realized that the voids were left by the bodies of people who perished when Mount Vesuvius erupted in 79 AD.

Fiorelli had an idea, an idea that would preserve the memory of these lives in a way never seen before. He began to pour plaster of Paris into the cavities, letting it harden, and then carefully removing the surrounding ash. What emerged were hauntingly detailed casts of the victims in their final moments—some shielding loved ones, others curled in anguish, all of them frozen in time!

And even though the bodies are no longer there, not everything disappeared! Bones, teeth, and sometimes fragments of jewelry remain encased within the plaster.

snippet.title: Pompeii AI Reconstruction: The Eruption That Stopped Time

Step inside the deadliest natural disaster of the ancient world. Using forensic AI reconstruction, we walk the streets of Pompeii on August 24th, 79 AD, tracing the final, terrifying hours of the city buried by Mount Vesuvius. This deep-dive documentary explores the sequence of events that led to the city's demise, starting with the initial pumice rain that encouraged a false sense of security, and culminating in the devastating pyroclastic surge. 

For 1,700 years, Vesuvius lay dormant, allowing the people of Pompeii to thrive without knowing they were farming on a ticking bomb. We reveal the crucial reasons why approximately 90% of the population escaped, and examine the fatal decisions made by the remaining 2,000 residents who chose to stay behind—mistaking the ash fall for a survivable storm. Learn about the extraordinary infrastructure of this Roman resort town, the preserved graffiti that acts as the ancient world's social media, and the scientific ignorance that cost Pliny the Elder his life. We break down the science of the eruption, from the collapse of the Plinian column to the speed and temperature of the pyroclastic flow—a thermal shock so intense death was nearly instantaneous. Discover the haunting story behind the famous plaster casts created by Giuseppe Fiorelli, eternalizing the final moments of the victims. 

This is not just history; it's a preserved snapshot of human life and a stark reminder that some things never change. Don't forget to like this video and subscribe to the channel for more history documentaries that bring the past back to life!

snippet.title: The Killers Left the Gold. For 1,500 Years, No One Came Back.
snippet.description:
Around the year 480 AD, on the island of Öland off the coast of Sweden, an entire village
was massacred in a single night. The attackers cut down men and children in their doorways,
in the streets, in their homes — and then did something no one has ever been able to explain.

They left the gold. They left the food cooking on the fires. They left the bodies where they fell.

Sandby Borg was a ringfort: a great oval wall of stone, four metres high, sheltering over
fifty houses — built in the chaos after Rome began to fall. One evening its gate was forced,
and what happened inside was not a battle. It was an execution. The dead were struck from
behind and from above, as they ran, as they knelt. One old man fell dying across his own
hearth and burned there.

And then — nothing. No looting. In five different houses, archaeologists found treasure the
killers simply walked past: gilded silver brooches, glass beads from the Continent, silver
rings. In the hearths, lamb and herring were still cooking.

Strangest of all: nobody ever buried the dead. On a small island where everyone knew everyone,
the fort was simply avoided — for fifteen hundred years — as if the ground itself had been
declared cursed. Archaeologists only went in around 2010, when looters threatened the site.
They found a moment frozen in time: an Iron-Age Pompeii. Twenty-six victims so far — and less
than ten percent of the fort has been excavated. Dozens of houses are still sealed under the
turf, with whatever, and whoever, is still inside them.

Who kills an entire village but refuses to take its gold? And why did no one ever come back?

This is File 23. Still sealed.

Pompeii was not simply buried and forgotten — it was a thriving, deeply complicated Roman city that had already survived earthquakes, political upheaval, and civic violence long before Vesuvius ever stirred.

This is the complete history of Pompeii: from its origins as a small Oscan settlement on a volcanic plain to its rise as one of the most commercially powerful towns in the Roman world. You will watch it absorb Greek culture, fall under Roman conquest, erupt in social violence, and rebuild itself into something extraordinary — only to be erased in under a single day.

The eruption of 79 AD unfolded over nearly twenty hours, giving thousands of people real choices and real chances. Understanding why so many stayed, and why so many died, reveals something deeply unsettling about human nature under pressure. What is often missed is how the city's centuries of layered history shaped the very conditions that made the catastrophe so lethal.

Pompeii's story does not end with ash. Since its rediscovery in the eighteenth century, every generation has used it as a mirror — projecting its own fears, its own ideals, and its own obsession with impermanence onto the ruins. From the Roman Republic and the Italian tribes of ancient Campania to the volcanic geology of the Bay of Naples and the ongoing excavations still rewriting what we know, this is history at its most vivid and most haunting.

snippet.title: Three Ancient Surgical Tools Nobody Can Explain
snippet.description:
Three surgical tools from the ancient world that worked — and that nobody can explain.
Peruvian surgeons drilling into living skulls with stone tools achieved a 91% survival rate by 1100 AD, outperforming American Civil War doctors by a wide margin with no anesthesia and no record of how they prevented infection. 
An Indian surgeon in 600 BC documented 125 specialized instruments for rebuilding a human nose using a forehead flap technique still used by plastic surgeons today, virtually unchanged. 
Bronze needles buried at Pompeii in 79 AD were precision-engineered to enter a living eye and displace a cataract lens — with no optical theory behind them — and the technique remained standard practice for 1,800 years.

snippet.description:
The last full day of Pompeii, hour by hour - 24 hours before Vesuvius erupted in 79 AD, rebuilt frame by frame with AI reconstruction.

On an ordinary autumn day in 79 AD, the people of Pompeii had no word for "volcano." Vesuvius had been silent for 1,800 years - just a green mountain covered in vineyards. Then it opened.

This is the last 24 hours of Pompeii, hour by hour. The eruption column rising 30 kilometers into the sky. The rain of pumice. The impossible choice to run or wait. The admiral Pliny the Elder sailing toward the disaster to rescue strangers. The darkness "as if the lamp had been put out in a closed room." And the pyroclastic surge that reached the city at dawn — the real killer no one saw coming.

Most of Pompeii escaped. Around 2,000 people stayed. This is the story of why.

snippet.title: TENOCHTITLAN 1519: The Greatest City The Spanish Erased From History (AI Reconstruction)
snippet.description:
TENOCHTITLAN. 1519.

A city of 200,000 to 300,000 people built in the middle of a lake.

Larger than London. Larger than Paris. Larger than any city in Europe.

Its streets were cleaner than anything in the western world. Its market served 60,000 people every single day. Its floating gardens turned an entire lake into farmland. Every child — boy and girl — went to school.

And then Hernán Cortés arrived. With 400 soldiers, horses the Aztecs had never seen, and a disease they had no immunity to.

Within two years — the greatest city in the western world was rubble.

This is what Tenochtitlan really looked like. Before the Spanish destroyed it.

snippet.title: Archaeologists make ‘once-in-a-century’ discovery at Pompeii | BBC News
snippet.description:
A "once-in-a-century" find has been unearthed in Pompeii after lying hidden for more than 2,000 years.
 
Archaeologists discovered a private bathhouse - potentially the largest ever found there - complete with hot, warm and cold rooms, exquisite artwork, and even a huge plunge pool.
 
The skeletons of a woman and a man were found in the house - the former discovered clutching a bag of coins and jewellery.
 
They had barricaded themselves into a small room, but were killed as a tsunami of superheated volcanic gas and ash - known as a pyroclastic flow - ripped through the town.

snippet.title: Pompeii: Before the Disaster (AI Reconstruction)
snippet.description:
Basically, in this video, I use AI to "resurrect" Pompeii and walk its streets exactly as they were in 79 AD, right before the disaster. It’s not just about looking at buildings; we explore life in the Forum, the Temples, and the Villa of the Mysteries at their peak, contrasting that vibrant reality (the colors, the people, the intact architecture) with the silent ruins that remain today.

We also break down the exact moment Vesuvius woke up and how that "mountain," which everyone thought was harmless, buried an entire city in a matter of hours. It’s crazy to see what was actually lost beneath the ash.

snippet.title: A City Frozen in Ash… Rebuilt by AI | The Last Day of Pompeii
snippet.description:
Step into a city that died in a single day… and came back to life through data and AI.

This documentary-style video takes you inside Pompeii on October 24th, 79 AD – not as ruins, but as a living, breathing Roman city. Using archaeological research, 3D scans and AI reconstruction, we follow an ordinary citizen through his “last normal day” before Mount Vesuvius erupts.

You’ll see:

How AI helps rebuild lost streets, homes and bathhouses

What everyday life actually felt like in an ancient Roman city

The hidden social divide between the rich villas and cramped slave quarters

How modern technology is preserving Pompeii as the real ruins slowly disappear

This is not just the story of one destroyed city.
It’s a warning… and a mirror for our own world today.

snippet.title: Salamis — How 371 Greek Ships Broke a 1,200 Ship Persian Invasion
snippet.description:
In September 480 BC, the Persian Empire put 1,200 warships into a narrow channel of water and lost them in a single afternoon — to a Greek fleet of 371. Five months later, the largest invasion the ancient world had ever assembled was retreating across a frozen river, half its men dead.

This is the battle that ended Persian westward expansion. Not Marathon ten years earlier. Marathon was the warning. Salamis was the answer. The moment the largest empire in the ancient world learned the limit of what could be taken by force.

The numbers tell only part of the story. Persia outnumbered Greece in ships, men, gold, and experienced commanders. In a strait one nautical mile wide, none of that mattered. Only geometry mattered. And one Athenian general — Themistocles — understood the geometry in a way the Persian king did not.

This episode breaks down the battle tactically: the silver strike at Laurion that built the Athenian fleet, the evacuation of Athens, the deception Themistocles sent to Xerxes the night before, the moment the Greek line reversed and rammed. And it places Salamis in the larger Persian arc — the empirical proof of what Cyrus understood and Xerxes forgot.
